profile.feeling: The first word you say about yourself; plain and neutral, never rude.

senses.def: my (before relatives and close relations: 我妈妈)
(formal, written) we; our — 我国 ‘our country’, 我校 ‘our school’

examples.tr: Our country has a large population.

phrases.tr: I walk my way, I keep my ways
phrases.meaning: to go one’s own way regardless of what others say
a life-and-death struggle

synonyms.nuance: ‘this person’: I, the undersigned — official statements and forms
everyday ‘I’ in much of the north (Shandong, Hebei, the northeast)
Classical Chinese ‘I’; today only in set phrases and jokingly

etymology.text: Originally a pictogram of a trident-like weapon or tool; borrowed for its sound to write the pronoun ‘I’ already in the oracle-bone script. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *ŋa.

funFacts: The character 我 was first a drawing of a weapon with a toothed blade; it only stands for ‘I’ because the words sounded alike.
pitfalls: 我 is both ‘I’ and ‘me’ — no case change: 他喜欢我 ‘he likes me’.
‘My’ is 我的 + noun (我的菜); 的 is dropped only before relatives and close relations (我妈妈, 我朋友).
Third-tone sandhi: 我很好 wǒ hěn hǎo is spoken wó hén hǎo (written tones stay).
subtleties: Chinese leaves out 我 when it is obvious: asked 你喜欢吗？ you can answer just 喜欢。
In formal writing 我 can mean ‘our’: 我国 (our country), 我校 (our school).

profile.feeling: The everyday, friendly ‘you’ — between equals, friends, younger people.

phrases.meaning: to compete eagerly, each trying to outdo the other

phrases.tr: you a word, I a phrase
phrases.meaning: everybody chiming in (a lively discussion)

synonyms.nuance: polite ‘you’ for elders, teachers, customers and strangers
‘Your Excellency’: very formal, diplomatic or ironic
Classical Chinese ‘you’

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 亻 (‘person’) + phonetic 尔. A colloquial form of 爾 (‘you’) attested since the Tang dynasty; ultimately from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *na-ŋ.

funFacts: 你好 is the textbook greeting, but friends usually greet each other with a name or a question instead.
pitfalls: To elders, teachers and customers use 您, not 你.
你们 is the plural ‘you’; there is no case or gender change in speech.
subtleties: In Taiwan the character 妳 is sometimes written for ‘you’ addressing a woman; Mainland Chinese writes 你 for everyone.

profile.feeling: Respect and courtesy — the waiter, the teacher, the grandparent.

examples.tr: Teacher, would you like some tea?

collocations.tr: take care (to a guest who is leaving)

synonyms.nuance: the ordinary ‘you’ — between equals and friends
very formal, diplomatic ‘you’

etymology.text: Ideogrammic compound of 你 (‘you’) + 心 (‘heart’). First attested in Jin/Yuan-era literature (also written 恁); usually explained as a fusion of 你們 (nǐmen, ‘you (plural)’), the polite use developing from the plural.

funFacts: The character puts 心 ‘heart’ under 你 ‘you’ — a handy memory aid: ‘you, from the heart’.
pitfalls: Used with friends or family, 您 can sound cold or sarcastic.
您们 is avoided by many speakers; for a polite plural say 各位 (‘everyone’) or 你们.
subtleties: 您 is most at home in Beijing and northern speech; many southern speakers use it mainly in service language and writing.

profile.feeling: Neutral third person; in writing the default for ‘someone’.

senses.def: other, another (in words like 他人, 其他)

examples.text: 不要随便拿他人的东西。
examples.tr: Don't just take other people's things.
examples.py: Bú yào suíbiàn ná tārén de dōngxi.

phrases.tr: stones from another hill can polish jade
phrases.meaning: advice from others can help you improve

synonyms.nuance: written ‘his, her, its, their’ (其中, 其他)
rare Beijing respectful ‘he/she’

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 亻 (‘man’) + phonetic 也; a corrupted form of 佗. The modern sense ‘he, she, it’ arose after the Han period in colloquial texts.

funFacts: Until about 1920 他 covered ‘she’ too; the separate character 她 is a 20th-century creation.
pitfalls: 他 and 她 are both pronounced tā — only writing tells them apart.
A mixed group is 他们, even if most of them are women.
subtleties: When the sex is unknown or does not matter, writing traditionally uses 他.

profile.feeling: Neutral; the same sound as ‘he’, a different character.

synonyms.nuance: used for women too when the sex does not matter or in older texts
Classical and early modern written ‘he/she’

etymology.text: Semantic 女 (‘woman’) + 也, built on the model of 他. The character became the standard written ‘she’ in the 1920s.
etymology.src: character composition; history of the character

funFacts: The poet and linguist Liu Bannong (刘半农) championed 她 around 1920 in his poem 教我如何不想她 (‘How can I not think of her’).
pitfalls: Spoken tā is ambiguous: in speech context tells you whether it is ‘he’ or ‘she’.
她们 only for an all-female group.
subtleties: In poetic and patriotic writing 她 can refer to the motherland (祖国) or other personified things.

profile.feeling: Neutral group feeling; the listener may or may not be included.

senses.def: (academic writing) we, referring to the author(s)

examples.text: 本文中我们讨论三个问题。
examples.tr: In this paper we discuss three questions.
examples.py: Běnwén zhōng wǒmen tǎolùn sān ge wèntí.

synonyms.nuance: inclusive ‘we’ (you and I) — warm, northern
northern colloquial ‘we’
written, old-fashioned ‘we’

etymology.text: 我 (‘I’) + the plural suffix 们, which is used with pronouns and nouns for people.
etymology.src: morphemes: 我 + plural suffix 们

funFacts: Chinese has only one plural ending for pronouns: 我们, 你们, 他们 — the same 们 everywhere.
pitfalls: 们 is not a general plural: 我们, 学生们 — but never *西红柿们.
我们 may exclude the listener; when you mean ‘you and I’, northerners prefer 咱们.
subtleties: Before group nouns 的 is usually dropped: 我们学校 (our school), 我们公司 (our company).

profile.feeling: Warm and inclusive: ‘you and I together’.

senses.def: we; us (inclusive: the speaker and the listener)

collocations.tr: the two of us (you and I)

synonyms.nuance: the general ‘we’, inclusive or exclusive; the usual word in the south and in Taiwan
short northern form; can also mean ‘I’

etymology.text: 咱 + plural suffix 们. The character 咱 is written with 口 (‘mouth’) + 自 (‘self’).

funFacts: English has no single word for inclusive ‘we’; Chinese 咱们 makes the difference audible.
pitfalls: Never use 咱们 when the listener is not part of the group: 我们明天走，你呢？ (not *咱们).
Tone: zán (2nd tone).
subtleties: Typical of northern Mandarin; in the south and in Taiwan most people just say 我们.

profile.feeling: Neutral; the default ‘they’ for people.

synonyms.nuance: only for a group of women
for animals and things (often simply left out)

etymology.text: 他 (‘he’) + plural suffix 们.
etymology.src: morphemes: 他 + plural suffix 们

funFacts: In speech 他们, 她们 and 它们 sound exactly the same: tāmen.
pitfalls: One man in the group → 他们.
For things, Chinese usually repeats the noun or leaves the pronoun out rather than saying 它们.
subtleties: 他们 also works generically: 他们说… ‘they say…, people say…’.

profile.feeling: Neutral; marks an all-female group in writing.

synonyms.nuance: the general ‘they’ — required as soon as one man is in the group

etymology.text: 她 (‘she’) + plural suffix 们.
etymology.src: morphemes: 她 + plural suffix 们

funFacts: A class of 30 girls and 1 boy is 他们 in standard usage.
pitfalls: Only for groups made up entirely of women or girls.
subtleties: Sounds identical to 他们: the difference exists only in writing.

profile.feeling: The plain ‘is’ that links two nouns; as an answer, a firm ‘yes, that’s right’.

senses.def: to be (links two nouns: A is B)
emphasis: it is … that (the 是……的 construction)

examples.tr: It was by plane that I came.
examples.py: Wǒ shì zuò fēijī lái de.

collocations.tr: is it or not? isn’t it?

phrases.meaning: to be practical and realistic, judge by the facts
to be opinionated and self-righteous

synonyms.nuance: wéi: ‘to be, to act as’ in written style (他被选为班长)
‘is, is indeed’ in classical and very formal writing (乃是)

etymology.text: Origin unclear. In Classical Chinese 是 was a pronoun ‘this’; the development ‘this > be right, correct > to be’ gave the copula, which emerged by the Eastern Han dynasty.

funFacts: In Classical Chinese 是 meant ‘this’ — the modern ‘is’ grew out of the pronoun.
pitfalls: No 是 before adjectives: 西红柿很红 (the tomato is red), not *西红柿是红.
The negation is always 不是 (bú shì), never *没是.
As ‘yes’, 是 fits questions with 是 or confirms a statement; to 你要吗？ answer 要。, to 你有吗？ answer 有。
subtleties: 是 can also say what fills a place: 桌子上都是书 ‘the table is covered with books’.
是的 is a softer, very common ‘yes’; a bare 是 can sound like ‘Yes, sir’.
To agree with what someone just said, 对 (duì, ‘right, correct’) is the most common ‘yes’: 你是老师？— 对。

profile.feeling: Possession and existence — one of the busiest verbs.

senses.def: (colloquial, euphemistic: 有了) to be pregnant

examples.tr: There are lots of tomatoes here.

phrases.text: 有朋自远方来，不亦乐乎
phrases.tr: when friends come from afar, is it not a joy?
phrases.meaning: a classic welcome to visiting friends

phrases.tr: for one with a will, the matter is finally achieved
phrases.meaning: where there is a will, there is a way

synonyms.nuance: to possess (qualities, meaning, features): 具有意义
to own, hold (much or important things): 拥有财富

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 又 (a hand) + semantic 肉 (‘meat’, now written ⺼). Folk etymology reads it as a hand holding meat, hence ‘to have’.

funFacts: The folk etymology ‘a hand holding meat’ makes a good memory aid, even though the real analysis treats 又 as the sound element.
pitfalls: Negate only with 没: 我没有, never *我不有.
Under negation 一个 is normally dropped: 我没有南瓜 (I have no pumpkin).
subtleties: When a place comes first, 有 means ‘there is’: 冰箱里有黄瓜 ‘there are cucumbers in the fridge’.
有 + a noun can make an adjective: 有名 (famous), 有用 (useful), 有意思 (interesting).

profile.feeling: Central to social life: food is how people show care.

senses.def: to suffer, endure (吃苦, 吃亏)

examples.tr: He has suffered a lot since childhood.
examples.py: Tā cóngxiǎo chīle hěn duō kǔ.

phrases.meaning: to be jealous (in love)

phrases.tr: what you can't eat you'll carry away
phrases.meaning: you'll have to face the consequences

synonyms.nuance: classical word for eat; lives on in compounds (食物 food, 饮食 diet)
polite, said to guests: 请慢用 = enjoy your meal

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 口 (‘mouth’) + phonetic 乞.

funFacts: 吃了吗？(‘Have you eaten?’) is a greeting, like ‘How are you?’ — not an invitation to a meal.
pitfalls: Drinks take 喝, not 吃: 喝水, 喝茶 — and soup is drunk: 喝汤.
吃 is used where English says ‘take’: 吃药 (take medicine).
subtleties: 吃 + an experience = to undergo it: 吃苦 (endure hardship), 吃亏 (lose out), 吃惊 (be startled).

profile.feeling: Tea, water, soup — and, at a dinner table, often alcohol.

examples.tr: What would you like to drink?
I drink a lot of water every day.
examples.py: Wǒ měitiān hē hěn duō shuǐ.

phrases.meaning: to have nothing to eat; to go hungry

synonyms.nuance: yǐn: written ‘to drink’, alive in compounds (饮料 drinks, 饮酒 drinking)

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 口 (‘mouth’) + phonetic 曷. An innovative written form of 欱, from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *hwap (‘to drink’).

funFacts: Chinese eats soup with a spoon but still says 喝汤 ‘drink soup’.
pitfalls: Soup and porridge are ‘drunk’ in Chinese: 喝汤, 喝粥.
The same character is read hè in 喝彩 (hècǎi, ‘to cheer’) — a different word, ‘to shout’.
subtleties: At a dinner, 喝一杯 or just 喝 usually means alcohol: 你喝吗？ may be an offer of a drink.

profile.feeling: Markets, shopping, bargains.

senses.def: to buy off, bribe (in 收买, 买通)

examples.tr: He wants to buy a car.
examples.py: Tā xiǎng mǎi yí liàng chē.

phrases.tr: buy the box, return the pearl
phrases.meaning: to value the wrapping over the content

synonyms.nuance: written, official ‘to purchase’
only in compounds: 购物 (shopping), 网购 (online shopping)

etymology.text: Ideogrammic compound: 网 (‘net’) + 貝 (‘cowrie’ = money); simplified 买. Possibly from Proto-Sino-Tibetan *laj (‘to buy; to barter’).

funFacts: Many money words contain 貝/贝 (cowrie shell, early money): 买, 卖, 贵 (expensive), 货 (goods).
pitfalls: 买 mǎi (3rd tone) = buy, 卖 mài (4th tone) = sell; the extra 十 on top of 卖 means ‘sell’.
Traditional 買 has 貝 (money) at the bottom; the simplified form hides it.
subtleties: 买单 ‘to pay the bill’ came into Mandarin from Cantonese 埋单.

profile.feeling: Warm, positive; from liking food to having a crush.

senses.def: to like; to be fond of
to tend to, to have a habit of (doing something)

examples.tr: I like you. (I have feelings for you.)
He's always late (it's a habit of his).

phrases.tr: like the new, loathe the old
phrases.meaning: to be fickle; always chasing the new

synonyms.nuance: stronger: ‘to love’; colloquially also ‘to love doing’: 爱吃
written, ‘to be fond of’: 受到读者喜爱
‘to be keen on’, mainly the noun ‘hobby’

etymology.text: 喜 (‘joy, happy’) + 欢 (‘joyful, glad’): a compound of two words for joy.

funFacts: Both characters mean ‘joy’, so 喜欢 is literally ‘joy-joy’.
pitfalls: Mainland standard has a neutral second syllable: xǐhuan; Taiwan says xǐhuān.
A verb follows directly — no ‘to’: 我喜欢吃玉米.
subtleties: 我喜欢你 is a typical way to confess feelings; 我爱你 is much heavier.
Degree words go before it: 很喜欢, 非常喜欢, 有点儿喜欢.

profile.feeling: Direct and practical: what you want, what is needed, what will happen.

senses.def: to want (to have); to ask for

examples.tr: It takes two hours to get to Beijing.
examples.py: Dào Běijīng yào liǎng ge xiǎoshí.

phrases.meaning: shameless

synonyms.nuance: softer, ‘would like to have’
‘to need’ — necessity rather than wish

etymology.text: Pictogram of a person with both hands at the waist; the original meaning was ‘waist’, now written 腰.

funFacts: The character once meant ‘waist’ — when it was borrowed for ‘want’, the flesh radical was added to make a new character 腰.
pitfalls: 不要 + verb is a command, ‘don’t!’: 不要吃! ‘Don’t eat (it)!’ For ‘I don’t want to eat’ say 我不想吃.
In 要求 (yāoqiú, ‘to demand’) the character is read yāo (1st tone).
subtleties: 要 is direct: at a counter 我要… is normal; to elders or hosts 我想要… sounds softer.
想 + verb = ‘would like to’ (a wish); 要 + verb = ‘want to, am going to’ (a firmer intention).

profile.feeling: Thinking, wishing, longing — soft and inward.

senses.def: to think; to think over; to suppose
to want to, would like to (+ verb)

examples.tr: I'd like to drink some water.
What would you like to eat?

examples.py: Wǒ xiǎng tā bú huì lái.

phrases.meaning: to let one’s imagination run wild; to worry needlessly
a fanciful, unrealistic idea

synonyms.nuance: more direct ‘want’, also ‘will’
‘to plan, intend’
‘to consider, hold the view that’
‘to hope’

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 相 (‘to look at’) + semantic 心 (‘heart, mind’) — to visualise, to think. From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *saŋ (‘to think’).

funFacts: 心 ‘heart’ is at the bottom of 想: in Chinese tradition the heart is the seat of thought.
pitfalls: 想 needs a verb before a thing: 我想吃土豆 / 我想要土豆. 想 + a person or place means ‘miss’: 我想你 ‘I miss you’.
‘I don’t want to’ is 我不想 — not 我不要 (which sounds like a refusal or a command).
subtleties: 想 = a wish (softer, may not happen); 要 = a firmer intention. 我想去 ‘I’d like to go’, 我要去 ‘I’m going to go’.

profile.feeling: Short, clear refusal or denial — the everyday ‘not’.

senses.def: not (negates verbs, adjectives and 是: habits, wishes, the present and the future)
cannot (between a verb and its complement: 听不懂)

phrases.meaning: shady, disreputable
see you there — I’ll wait until you come

synonyms.nuance: negates 有 and says that something did not happen
bié: ‘don’t!’ in commands
‘not, is not’ in written style (非卖品 ‘not for sale’)

etymology.text: Originally a pictogram of the calyx of a flower; borrowed for the negation. A new character 柎 was later made for ‘calyx’.

funFacts: The textbook says 不 (bù) has 4th tone, yet you will hear it as bú almost as often — before every 4th-tone syllable.
pitfalls: Tone sandhi: before a 4th tone 不 is said bú — 不是 bú shì, 不要 bú yào; in 听不懂 and A-not-A questions it is toneless.
Never 不有 — the negation of 有 is 没有.
For a past event use 没: 我昨天没去, not *我昨天不去.
subtleties: 不 can express will: 我不去 ‘I won’t go / I refuse to go’.
As an answer, Chinese prefers to repeat the verb: 你要吗？— 不要。 A bare 不 sounds blunt.

profile.feeling: Matter-of-fact: something is missing or did not happen.

senses.def: not (before 有; and before a verb: did not, has not)
(short for 没有) not have; there isn’t

examples.tr: He isn't as tall as you.

phrases.meaning: no way!
disrespectful of age and rank

synonyms.nuance: negates habits, wishes, the future, adjectives and 是
wú: ‘without, there is no’ in written style (无人 ‘nobody’)
wèi: ‘not yet’ in written style (未成年 ‘under age’)

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 水 (‘water’) + phonetic; the character’s old meaning is ‘to sink’. The negator méi is possibly a colloquial variant of 勿 or 未 influenced by 有 — not derived from ‘to sink’ (Schuessler).

funFacts: The traditional form 沒 has 𠬛 on the right; the simplified 没 writes 殳 (几 over 又) instead.
pitfalls: Never *没是 — the negation of 是 is 不是.
Don’t add 了 after 没 + verb: 我没吃 (not *我没吃了).
In 沉没 (chénmò, ‘to sink’) the same character is read mò.
subtleties: 没 describes facts, 不 describes will and habits: 我不吃肉 ‘I don’t eat meat’ vs 我没吃肉 ‘I didn’t eat (the) meat’.

profile.feeling: Pointing at what is near — physically or in the conversation.

synonyms.nuance: written ‘this’, in fixed words: 此外 (besides), 因此 (therefore)

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: semantic 辶 (‘walk’) + phonetic 言. Originally a verb ‘to meet’ (now read yàn); borrowed for ‘this’ through a medieval confusion with 遮 (zhē, ‘this’).

funFacts: 这 (zhè) ‘this’, 那 (nà) ‘that’ and 哪 (nǎ) ‘which’ form a set: 这里 here, 那里 there, 哪里 where?
pitfalls: Before a noun, 这 normally needs a measure word: 这个西红柿, 这根黄瓜.
Many northerners say zhèi before a measure word: 这个 zhèige.
subtleties: As a subject, 这 stands alone: 这是土豆 ‘this is a potato’ — no measure word.

profile.feeling: Curiosity — or, with the right tone, surprise and protest.

examples.tr: Would you like something to eat?
examples.py: Nǐ xiǎng chī diǎnr shénme ma?

phrases.meaning: what brings you here? (to an unexpected visitor)

synonyms.nuance: shá: northern colloquial ‘what’
written ‘what’: 何时 (when), 为何 (why)

etymology.text: A corruption of medieval 是物 (‘what’) or 什物 (‘miscellaneous items’), perhaps influenced by 何物 (‘what’).

funFacts: Taiwan usually writes 什麼 or 甚麼; both are traditional forms of 什么.
pitfalls: No 吗 with a 什么 question: 你喝什么？ — with 吗, 什么 means ‘anything’: 你喝什么吗？ ‘Will you drink anything?’
Word order does not change: put 什么 where the answer goes (你喝什么？— 我喝茶).
subtleties: Before a noun, 什么 asks ‘what kind / which’: 什么菜？ ‘what dish?’.
In fast speech it is often shéme.

override.pinyin: pinyin: Mainland dictionaries (Xiandai Hanyu Cidian) give nǎ·li with a toneless li; Wiktionary’s own entry lists this toneless variant ‘nǎli’, which the kaikki extraction garbles into “nálǐ] → nǎli (toneless final syllable variant)”, so the tool cannot match it. Everything else checked clean before this override was added.

profile.feeling: Asking for a place; and the classic modest reply to praise.

senses.def: (哪里哪里) not at all — a modest reply to a compliment

examples.text: 哪里哪里，我的中文还不好。
examples.tr: Not at all, my Chinese is still not good.
examples.py: Nǎli nǎli, wǒ de Zhōngwén hái bù hǎo.

synonyms.nuance: nǎr: the erhua form — everyday in Beijing and the north
‘what place’ — a little more explicit
written ‘where’

etymology.text: 哪 (‘which’) + 里 (‘place; inside’): ‘which place’.

funFacts: Answering a compliment with 哪里哪里 literally asks ‘where? where?’ — as if the praised quality cannot be found.
pitfalls: No 吗 with 哪里: 土豆在哪里？ (not *…吗？).
哪里 nǎli (where?) vs 那里 nàli (there): only the 口 radical and the tone differ.
Say 在哪里 for ‘where is’ — the verb 在 is needed: *土豆哪里？
subtleties: Both 哪里 and 哪儿 are standard: -儿 forms (哪儿, 这儿, 那儿) are typical of Beijing and the north, -里 forms of the south, Taiwan and writing.
Spoken: the 3rd tone of 哪 before 里 is usually heard as náli.

profile.feeling: Here, near the speaker.

synonyms.nuance: zhèr: the erhua form — everyday in Beijing and the north
written ‘here, at this point’ (signs, documents)
written ‘this place’

etymology.text: 这 (‘this’) + 里 (‘place; inside’): ‘this place’.

funFacts: Traditional characters are written two ways: 這裡 (Taiwan) and 這裏 (Hong Kong).
pitfalls: A place with 在 comes before the verb: 我在这里吃, not *我吃在这里.
这里 is a place word, not ‘this’: 这里的土豆 ‘the potatoes here’.
subtleties: ‘Here with me’ is pronoun + 这儿/这里: 你的书在我这儿 ‘your book is here with me’.
Mainland dictionaries give zhè·li with a toneless li.

profile.feeling: Neat and peaceful — the character also means ‘harmony’.

senses.def: peace; harmony (in words like 和平)

examples.tr: I'd like to have a meal with you.
examples.py: Wǒ xiǎng hé nǐ yìqǐ chīfàn.

examples.tr: We all hope for world peace.

synonyms.nuance: gēn: everyday ‘and, with’, especially in the north
yǔ: written ‘and’ (titles, documents: 《战争与和平》)
jí: ‘and, as well as’ before the last item of a formal list
tóng: ‘and, with’ in formal or southern usage

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 禾 + semantic 口 (‘mouth’) — harmony. The original form was 龢, with the flute radical 龠 suggesting harmony in music.

funFacts: 和 can also mean ‘Japanese’: 和服 (kimono), 和食 (Japanese cuisine).
pitfalls: 和 joins nouns, not sentences: ‘I eat and he drinks’ is 我吃，他喝 — not *我吃和他喝.
In a list of three, 和 goes only before the last item: 西红柿、黄瓜和土豆.
Other readings: hè (附和 ‘to echo’), huó (和面 ‘to knead dough’), hú (winning at mahjong).
subtleties: Verbs and adjectives are joined with 又…又…, 也 or 而且, not 和: 又便宜又新鲜 ‘cheap and fresh’.

lexemes.role: to be (located) at — the ‘be’ of place: 土豆在这里; also ‘at/in’ before a place and the progressive marker

profile.feeling: Where something is; where and when something happens.

senses.def: to be at, to be in (location)
at, in (before a place, in front of the verb)
in the middle of doing (progressive: 在吃饭)

synonyms.nuance: yú: written ‘at, in’ (生于北京 ‘born in Beijing’)
wèiyú: ‘to be located at’ (descriptions, documents)

etymology.text: Phono-semantic compound: phonetic 才 + phonetic 士; 士 was later corrupted into 土 (‘earth’). In the oracle bones 才 alone was borrowed for this word.

funFacts: The progressive use (他在吃饭 ‘he is eating’) grew out of the place meaning — literally ‘he is at eating’.
pitfalls: Known thing + 在 + place: 西红柿在这里 ‘the tomatoes are here’. Place + 有 + new thing: 这里有西红柿 ‘there are tomatoes here’.
Negate with 不: 他不在 ‘he isn’t in’.
subtleties: 在 + place goes before the verb: 我在家吃饭, not *我吃饭在家.

lexemes.role: question particle: put at the end of a statement, it makes a yes/no question (你要黄瓜吗？); toneless
the number one; with a measure word it plays the role of “a” (一个南瓜); tone changes: yí before a 4th tone, yì before the others
the general measure word (一个土豆, 这个西红柿); often toneless after numbers
measure word for long, thin things: 一根黄瓜, 一根胡萝卜, 一根葱
measure word for small round things: 一颗洋葱, 一颗豌豆
measure word for plants: 一棵生菜, 一棵菠菜, 一棵卷心菜
measure word for long, narrow (often flexible) things: 一条茄子, 一条鱼, 一条路
measure word for heads of garlic (一头大蒜) and for livestock

absent.reason: Chinese has no articles. A known thing is a bare noun, usually placed before the verb (西红柿在这里 ‘the tomatoes are here’); when pointing is needed, 这/那 + measure word (这个西红柿).
absent.use: bare noun (often before the verb); 这/那 + measure word when it must be explicit

absent.reason: No indefinite article. A bare noun is often enough (这是西红柿 ‘this is a tomato’); to introduce one new thing, Chinese uses 一 + measure word (我买一个南瓜 ‘I buy a pumpkin’).
absent.use: 一 + measure word + noun (一个, 一根, 一棵 …)
